name: shea2023_covid_models
citation: Shea K, Borchering RK, Probert WJM, Howerton E, Bogich TL, Li S-L, van Panhuis WG, Viboud C, et al. (2023) Multiple models for outbreak decision support in the face of uncertainty. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 120(18):e2207537120
licence: CC BY 4.0 (article and Dataset S2). The authors' repository github.com/MMODS-org/Elicitation-1 is GPL-3: nothing is translated from its code; the aggregation is written from the description in the article
retrieved: 2026-11-25, article PDF, SI Appendix and Datasets S1 and S2 supplied by the user; the round 2 submissions were converted from Dataset S2 (pnas.2207537120.sd02.xlsx, one sheet for each model) by a script, keeping each value as stored
decision: When to reopen non-essential workplaces in a generic US county of 100,000 people on 15 May 2020, projected to 15 November 2020 by 17 models from 16 groups
unit: infections, deaths, peak hospital beds occupied, probability of an outbreak, and days with workplaces closed, each as the models projected it; no outcome is valued in money
baseline_note: 'open', immediate reopening on 15 May, is the option without restrictions

action_names.closed: workplaces closed throughout the six months
action_names.5percent: reopen when cases fall below 5% of the peak
action_names.2weeks: reopen two weeks after the peak

weights: Each of the 16 groups has equal weight; the group that submitted two models (G.1 and G.2) has its weight divided between them (Materials and Methods)
aggregation: 'Aggregate results were produced by taking a weighted average of the individual CDFs' (a linear opinion pool). Here each submission's distribution function is taken as linear between the quantiles given, and a pooled quantile is found by bisection.

dataset_s2.provenance: Dataset S2, round 2 submissions: for each model, intervention and objective, the quantiles requested (1 to 100; model F gives 0 to 100 and model H 1 to 99; models G.1, G.2 and K give the probability of an outbreak as a single number)

targets.where: Results, first paragraph: 'from 48,100 (48.1% of the county population) in the open intervention'
Results, first paragraph: 'to 8,527 in the closed intervention'
targets.resolution: Ours is 8,530: the pooled distribution is interpolated between the quantiles given, and the authors' interpolation differs in detail. Dataset S2's own aggregate sheet has 8,526.6.

targets.where: Results, first paragraph: 'reduced median cumulative infections by 82%'
Results, 'Model Projections Are Comparable with Real-World Data': 'median deaths 73; 50% IQR, 12 to 228'
Results: 'nonessential workplaces were closed for 184 d'
Results: 'closed for a median of 129 and 96 d'
Results: '34% vs. 11% chance of exceedance based on the aggregate results'
targets.resolution: Ours are 33.4% and 10.0%, read from the pooled distribution at 200 beds; within the interpolation.

targets.where: Results, first paragraph: 'the probability of an outbreak was high (aggregate median, 71%)'
targets.resolution: Not reproduced. The submissions for this outcome are of different kinds: some models give one probability, some give a list of zeros and ones (one for each simulated run), and one gives a distribution of probabilities, so a median of the pooled values depends on how the zeros and ones are interpolated. Taking each model's probability as the mean of what it submitted, the weighted mean over models is 0.47, and the models at 0.23 or below carry exactly half of the weight, the next being at 0.42. The published 71% (0.714 in Dataset S2's aggregate sheet) is above both.

targets.where: Results: 'cumulative infections for the full reopening strategy ranged widely, despite all models ranking the intervention as worst'

not_replicated.items: The round 1 results and the comparison of rounds (Fig. 2), the comparison with reported county deaths (Fig. 3), and the supplementary figures
not_replicated.reason: The case study is about the decision; it uses the final (round 2) projections only.
